Against the odds, Nolan Arenado is a 30-home run hitter for the Diamondbacks
Arenado joined a short list of third basemen with eight different 30-home run seasons, with the benchmark of 400 for his career within reach next season.
(Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images)
SAN DIEGO — Nolan Arenado hit 28 home runs combined over the previous two seasons before the Arizona Diamondbacks traded for the third baseman last offseason.
Defense and leadership were the baseline expectations for Arenado in Arizona, and whatever was left in the tank offensively was bonus.
In his age 35 campaign, Arenado has clubbed 30 home runs, punishing a hanging slider from San Diego Padres pitcher Casey Mize on Friday to hit a mark he had not reached since 2022. That year, Arenado was a finalist for the National League MVP with the St. Louis Cardinals.
He has experienced some quieter times since then, suggesting he declined to the point where he could no longer be relied on as an impact bat for a lineup.
The potential future Hall of Famer has reversed time this season for a team that has sorely needed the production.
“It meant a lot,” Arenado told Arizona Sports after hitting his 30th home run. “Just from where I started and just where I’ve been the last couple of years. It hasn’t been easy, but I just thank God that I’ve been healthy. And I owe a lot of credit to the hitting coaches for challenging me and all these guys for challenging me to take chances and work on things.”
Nolan Arenado is on a HEATER!
9 HR in September, 30 HR on the season 😯 pic.twitter.com/1ZcIDpDnmo
— MLB (@MLB) September 26, 2026
Arenado was visibly amped running the bases after the blast that put the D-backs ahead 6-2 in a must-win game they would take 11-4. The Southern California native also did it in front of his parents and brother, who made the hour drive south to watch him play.
“That was really cool,” Arenado said.
This is the eighth time Arenado has hit 30 home runs in a season. 28 players all-time have more such seasons and only two while spending most of their time at third base, per Stathead: Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12) and Eddie Mathews (10).
Arenado did so from 2015-19 and picked the streak back up after the shortened 2020 campaign in 2021-22.
This is the outlier outside his prime, especially after he hit 12 home runs last season.
“He has regained a lot of that offensive magic that’s been with him for so long,” manager Torey Lovullo said.
When asked about his offense’s recent success, Diamondbacks general manager Mike Hazen said on Friday, “We’re hitting more home runs. Arenado’s hitting a home run every night.”
Arenado has homered nine times in September, second in Major League Baseball to Baltimore’s Pete Alonso (11). He owns an .889 OPS in the second half of this season. And his four home runs in the past five games have come at a time when the Diamondbacks have had to win to keep their playoff hopes alive.
Arenado joked on the Diamondbacks TV broadcast Friday night that he is probably making Arizona’s hitting coaches work harder than they ever had before. He gave hitting coach Joe Mather a big hug in the dugout after going yard.
Arenado came to Arizona with a reputation of being a maniacal competitor and worker.
He has aimed to challenge himself during his preparation before games to get his body up to speed at this age, not totally dissimilar to Eugenio Suarez when he turned around his 2024 season in Arizona. The veteran has said lately he has cooled off the pregame physical work to maintain his body this late in the season, which has paid off.
Health has also been a factor, as Arenado dealt with shoulder issues at the end of his St. Louis tenure that he felt hampered him. He has been banged up in the second half of this season (intercostal, thumb) but has managed to limit his time off the field.
Before Friday’s game, Arenado stood in the batter’s box with his headphones and a bat, practicing his load and stride. Nobody was throwing batting practice yet, and there were still tamps and other grounds-keeping equipment on the field. Perhaps he was visualizing what soon became reality when he shot a ball into the Western Metal Supply Co. building.
Lars Nootbaar has had a front-row seat to Arenado’s career since he came up with the Cardinals in 2021, reuniting with the veteran at this past trade deadline.
“I just think that if anybody saw what he does and what he goes through on a daily basis and to try to get himself in a good position and be as obsessive as he is and be as passionate as he is, to get rewarded in this game and to be able to hit 30 in front of his family, that’s really cool from a baseball fan perspective and friend,” Nootbaar said.
Geraldo Perdomo predicted this re-breakout season back in spring training, and he claims to have called Arenado going for 30 home runs a couple weeks ago.
“I’m happy for him,” Perdomo said. “He’s the type of player who works every day hard in the cages with the hitting coaches to get better.”
Arenado enters Saturday second among qualified D-backs hitters with an .803 OPS, ahead of Corbin Carroll and Ketel Marte and trailing Gabriel Moreno.
He has previously been candid about wishing he has had more success this year with runners in scoring position, a shortcoming for large chunks of the season both individually and team-wide. He is batting .228 in those spots, although the OPS has climbed to .745.
This is not quite the MVP-candidate version of Arenado’s prime, but there is no doubt that the Diamondbacks acquiring him from St. Louis without having to pay the majority of his contract was a steal. It is arguably the biggest win of Hazen’s offseason.
Arenado is up to 383 career home runs, as the celebrated 400 benchmark is within grasp in 2027. MLB also revealed the 20 top-selling jerseys for the 2026 season, and Arenado was 19th on the list, the highest Diamondback.
For now and most importantly, with the D-backs trailing the final NL Wild Card spot by one game with two to play, can Arenado push this hot streak a couple games further?

Pete Alonso nunca ha temido decir lo que piensa. El viernes, el poderoso bateador de los Orioles encontró una nueva forma de recordar al mundo del béisbol una de las frases más memorables de sus tensas negociaciones contractuales con los Mets.
Horas antes de la doble cartelera de Baltimore contra los Yankees, se vio a Alonso vistiendo una camiseta que incluía una cita ya convertida en parte de la historia de los Mets.
Fabricada por la empresa de ropa deportiva BreakingT, la camiseta celebra el jonrón número 300 en la carrera de Alonso, pero también destaca la frase que, según se informa, le dijo a David Stearns, presidente de operaciones de béisbol de los Mets, durante las negociaciones posteriores a la temporada 2024: "Cuando evalúen mi carrera para el Salón de la Fama dentro de unos años, tú seguirás jugueteando con tus jodidas fórmulas".
Alonso está brillando con los Orioles
El comentario, reportado inicialmente por Jon Heyman en mayo, surgió durante un periodo de conflicto entre Alonso y la directiva de los Mets. En aquel entonces, el jugador seleccionado cinco veces para el Juego de Estrellas venía de lo que se consideraba una temporada floja para sus estándares, registrando un promedio de bateo de .240, 34 jonrones y un OPS de .788 en 2024.
A pesar de la baja en su rendimiento, Alonso seguía siendo uno de los bateadores de poder más destacados del béisbol y buscaba un contrato que reflejara ese estatus. Pete ejerció su opción de salida y se convirtió nuevamente en agente libre. Esta vez, el resultado fue distinto.
El invierno pasado firmó un contrato de cinco años y 155 millones de dólares con los Orioles, poniendo fin a su larga etapa en Queens e iniciando un nuevo capítulo en Baltimore. Si la camiseta del viernes pretendía servir como recordatorio de aquella saga, Alonso lo respaldó con el tipo de actuación que ha definido su primera temporada con los Orioles.
Una temporada de debut impresionante en Baltimore
El poderoso bateador conectó dos jonrones en la victoria de Baltimore por 10-2 sobre los Yankees, incluido un descomunal batazo de 471 pies en la séptima entrada. El batazo igualó el segundo jonrón más largo de sus ocho años de carrera en las Grandes Ligas y reforzó aún más su reputación como uno de los bateadores de poder más temidos del juego.
Esta actuación también se suma a lo que ha sido una impresionante temporada de debut en Baltimore. Tras un comienzo lento, Alonso se ha consolidado como una pieza clave en la alineación de los Orioles; llegó a la jornada con una línea ofensiva de .267/.363/.522 y liderando la Liga Americana con 43 cuadrangulares.
Según se informa, los Mets ofrecieron un acuerdo valorado en unos 40 millones de dólares por dos años. Las negociaciones se tornaron tensas, pero ambas partes finalmente llegaron a un acuerdo: un contrato de dos años y 54 millones de dólares que incluía una cláusula de rescisión tras la temporada 2025.
Para Baltimore, ese rendimiento es precisamente la razón por la que la organización decidió invertir a largo plazo en el veterano primera base. Para Alonso, es una prueba más de que su poderío ofensivo sigue estando entre lo mejor del deporte. El momento en que se produjo este despliegue de fuerza el viernes resultó especialmente significativo, dado el reciente regreso de Alonso a Nueva York.
A principios de este mes, recibió una cálida acogida en el Citi Field cuando los Orioles visitaron a los Mets. Durante la serie, Alonso conectó el jonrón número 300 de su carrera ante su excompañero Kodai Senga; empató el partido en la novena entrada y provocó que los aficionados de los Mets lo aclamaran para que saliera a saludar. Aquel momento recordó que, a pesar de las disputas contractuales y su posterior salida, el vínculo de Alonso con Nueva York sigue siendo fuerte.

item.content:encoded:
This just in, ladies and gentlemen: Pete Alonso is really good at baseball.
The Most Valuable Oriole continued to be the best thing to happen to this franchise in a long time, adding two more homers to his league-leading total in a 10-2 blowout win to open a doubleheader against the Yankees.
Whatever other things have gone wrong for the Orioles this year — and oh boy, are there many — Pete Alonso has been worth the price of admission all by himself. Tonight, even in a game that had no meaning for either team, he proved why.
Alonso stepped to the plate with a man aboard in the third against Yankees starter Brendan Beck, who'd begun the game with two scoreless innings. Pete put an end to that real quick. He drove a 407-foot dinger into the left-field seats, his 42nd of the year. At that point, Alonso's last seven hits had all been dingers. Did I mention this guy is good at baseball?
The Orioles turned the game into a laugher in the fourth even without Pete being prominently involved (though he did get a single). The O's loaded the bases with nobody out for the soft underbelly of the lineup, including Christian Franklin and Carlos Narváez, who entered the game with a combined zero RBIs in 132 plate appearances with the Orioles. That's Caleb Joseph territory right there. Franklin managed to get off the schneid with a sharp single to right, collecting his first major league RBI, but Narváez remained in his drought by hitting into a force at the plate.
It shouldn't be that hard to get one measly RBI, Carlos. Just watch as Dylan Beavers gets four of them in one at-bat! The O's right fielder jumped on a hanging curveball from Beck and clobbered it into the right-field seats for his first career grand slam. Beavers! With one mighty swing, the Orioles had an insurmountable 7-0 lead.
The Birds' victory was all but assured, but that doesn't mean they couldn't have some more fun along the way. In the top of the sixth, Jeremiah Jackson lofted a fly ball to deep center field. Spencer Jones loped back at an ambling pace, as if he had the ball tracked all the way, but when he reached up to make the catch, it glanced off his glove and deflected to the wall. The ball trickled along the warning track for so long that Jackson just kept circling the bases, and by the time the Yankees got the ball into the infield, Jackson had slid in safely with an inside-the-park home run.
Look at the wheels on Jeremiah! If you'd told me that the Orioles would have two inside-the-parkers this season and they'd be hit by Coby Mayo and Jeremiah Jackson, I'm not sure I would've believed you. This has been a strange season, occasionally in good ways.
You know what's not strange? Pete Alonso being awesome. It's just what he does, and always has. Alonso led off the seventh against reliever Yerry de los Santos and absolutely demolished a baseball. Holy smokes, was it tattooed, a mammoth blast the landed high into the left-field bleacher seats.
Pete, that baseball had a family! The blast was his second of the game and AL-leading 43rd of the year, and extended his AL-leading RBI count to 112. In all likelihood, Pete is going to take two of the three Triple Crown categories. He won't win AL MVP, and I'm not saying he should, but…is there any player in the American League who's really that much better than him? I'd put him in my top five for sure.
This game was all Orioles, but if there was one disappointing aspect, it's that Trevor Rogers didn't get the chance to earn the win in what may well have been his final start as an Oriole. Rogers pitched brilliantly tonight as always, but the Orioles, in an apparently pre-planned move, removed him from the game after four innings and 55 pitches.
I mean…why? Rogers was showing no signs of fatigue. He mowed down the Yankees in the first four frames, throwing 41 strikes and just 14 balls. He allowed only one run, on an Amed Rosario RBI single in the fourth, and the O's had a comfortable six-run lead when he left. Was his arm really going to fall off if he threw more than 55 pitches in his final start of the season?
I will grant that he'd already thrown a career-high 169.2 innings this season, and perhaps the Orioles saw no reason to push him in a meaningless game, but I would've let him at least pitch one more inning to get a W next to his name. Mostly I just don't want to accept that this might've been the last time we see Rogers in an Orioles uniform.
The Orioles hit double digits in runs on Gunnar Henderson's RBI single in the eighth that deflected off the second baseman, and the bullpen took it from there. Albert Suárez, now in his sixth stint with the Orioles this year, did his usual quality work in long relief. He tossed four scoreless innings and struck out five, even despite a nosebleed that afflicted him in the eighth. Suárez has been an unsung hero of the O's bullpen, constantly eating up innings without complaint even when he knows he'll probably get DFA'd the next day, then inevitably returning to the roster to do it all over again.
Alex Hoppe's ninth inning was a mess — 22 pitches, two walks, and a run — but a nine-run lead gives you plenty of wiggle room, and he eventually finished it with a called strikeout of Ben Rice. Orioles win, 10-2. Not a bad way to start the weekend.

NEW YORK (AP) — Pete Alonso homered twice to take over the American League lead with 43, including a 471-foot drive deep into the left field bleachers, and the Baltimore Orioles routed the New York Yankees 10-2 in a doubleheader opener on Friday.
Dylan Beavers had his first career grand slam in a five-run fourth and Jeremiah Jackson added an inside-the-park homer in the sixth.
Alonso hit rookie Brendan Beck's first-pitch slider in the third inning, becoming the first Oriole since Mark Trumbo in 2016 with seven straight hits that were homers.
Alonso singled in the fourth and three innings later hit a changeup at least halfway up the left field bleachers for a 9-1 lead, the fourth-longest homer in the major leagues this year.
Alonso moved out of a four-way tie for the AL home run lead. His 113 RBIs tied St. Louis' Alec Burleson for the big league high and the most by an Oriole since Chris Davis' 117 in 2015.
It was Alonso's 29th multi-homer game and third this year.
Beavers hit Baltimore's sixth grand slam this season, a drive into the right-field seats for a 7-0 lead.
Jackson added Baltimore’s second inside-the-park homer this year when he hit a fly ball that went over center fielder Spencer Jones’ glove at the warning track in front of New York’s bullpen. The ball caromed in front of the fence and Jackson crossed the plate ahead of right fielder Amed Rosario's throw.
Baltimore starter Trevor Rogers allowed one run and five hits in four innings. Albert Suárez (3-0) pitched four innings for the win.
Rosario had an RBI single for the Yankees, who honored Hall of Fame pitcher CC Sabathia by retiring his No. 52 and giving him a plaque in Monument Park in a pregame ceremony.
Anthony Volpe debuted at third base for the Yankees and had a double by Christian Encarnacion-Strand hit the bag go over his head in the ninth.
Beck (0-2) allowed seven runs and six hits in five innings.
Up Next
RHP Brandon Young (9-5, 3.62 ERA) starts for Baltimore in Game 2.

NEW YORK -- When the Orioles arrived at Yankee Stadium early Friday afternoon, it was the first time the team had convened since being eliminated from postseason contention. Baltimore’s playoff aspirations ended during Thursday’s off-day, when a White Sox win at Kansas City dropped the O’s postseason odds to 0%.
Manager Craig Albernaz addressed his players inside the visitors’ clubhouse prior to the start of the final three-game series vs. the Yankees -- one that doesn’t have any stakes.
“Obviously, we’re eliminated, and it’s not a place where we wanted to be. But we’re here, and it sucks. It’s something for myself, and also the rest of the team, we don’t want to have this feeling again,” Albernaz said. “I just challenged the guys that, first and foremost, I can be better for them. I’ve got to make adjustments and help us in the win column as much as I can, but also challenge them that each player do some self-reflection and figure out the little margins where they can get better as well and attack them this offseason.
“Us as a group, if we all attack those margins and you look up, next year, hopefully, we’ll be in a better spot.”
That was the general consensus among the Orioles. Everybody is disappointed about entering Friday with a 78-81 record and knowing their season won’t extend beyond Sunday. But there’s a belief that it won’t be like this again in 2027.
Pete Alonso has been Baltimore’s leader all season. After signing a five-year, $155 million deal last December, the 31-year-old slugger has not only been the team’s best player on the field, but he has become a strong presence with a loud voice inside the clubhouse.
And Alonso didn’t mince words when asked about Thursday’s elimination.
“That’s not the expectation. As a club, we failed to perform and do what we were supposed to do. We had great moments, great individual performances, but as a whole, that’s not the standard here. And that’s unacceptable for us,” Alonso said. “The standard for us is to not only make the postseason, but make a run and have a legitimate shot to hold up a trophy at the end of the year, and we didn’t even give ourselves an opportunity to enter the dance in October.”
After making consecutive postseason appearances in 2023 and ‘24, the O’s have missed the playoffs in both ‘25 and ‘26. There had been optimism for this season to be a bounce-back year, and instead, Baltimore never quite played up to expectations.
The Orioles never had a record above .500 after falling to 9-9 on April 15. They spent nearly the entire season with a losing record, then returned to .500 when they improved to 69-69 on Aug. 31. However, Baltimore opened September with six straight losses.
With the race for the third American League Wild Card wide open for the final few weeks of the season, the O’s stayed alive for longer than they likely would have in most years.
“I think if you ask anyone in this clubhouse, it didn’t really feel like we played our best baseball over a collective period of time -- pretty much the whole year,” outfielder Colton Cowser said. “It kind of sucks, because it did feel like it was somewhat of a down year in the AL. ... So I think when you reflect upon it like that, it feels like we probably didn’t take advantage of a year where we probably could have made the playoffs.”
So, where do the Orioles go from here?
They still have to wrap up the season in New York. Then, the players will head their separate ways and take some time to unwind and debrief early in the offseason.
There will be transactions made, whether that’s in free agency or via trades. The O’s will surely look at least slightly different when they begin play in the 2027 season.
But Baltimore still has confidence in the potential for a successful long-term future.
“I think this team can be in a really good spot next year,” Cowser said.
“Next year, whatever needs to happen, we need to do a better job. We need to do a better job as players, because that’s what it boils down to,” Alonso added. “The expectation is to be a great team.”

The best time for baseball failure Mike Elias to trade one of his failing former top draft picks is, invariably right now.
Because the longer they persist in his laughingstock player development strata – and the more they toil under what’s been a disaster medical and training staff - invariably their future value will decline and things will only get worse. Among Elias’s superpowers, wrecking top prospects is right up there with building third-grade rosters, hiring inane managers and constructing teams incapable of catching the ball or executing baseball fundamentals.
Which brings us to Jackson Holliday, Elias’s second first-overall selection (with his overt tank forcing even the craven and cynical billionaires who run baseball to change their draft rules), and why he needs to go this offseason. And to be clear Holliday needs to go ASAP as badly as Elias’s first overhyped first-overall pick, Adley Rutschman, needed to be jettisoned before the trade deadline. Long a Holliday skeptic myself – I begged and pleaded them to make him a cornerstone inn a Tarik Skubal package back in 2024 - I tried to keep an open mind that sweeping midseason stance and swing corrections might turn him around, but that was folly.
It’s time for him to be packaged (ideally with failed fifth-overall pick Colton Cowser as should have happened at the deadline) this winter.
This won’t get better here, and we have to operate now with the known constraints moving forward” Elias is as empowered as ever, overmatched puppet skipper Craig Albernaz is back for 2027, and the idea these mooks are going to turn Holliday into a winning centerfielder is ridiculous (though several top analysts believe it can be done). They couldn’t turn him into a competent second baseman after perpetual grifter Elias sold you he was a five-tool All Star shortstop when he drafted him.
Again, I watched him throughout the minors, called this out as an overhyped positionless prospect and begged them to sell him on him when the roster was a Skubal away from doing potential October damage. Alas, those days are gone and they’re not coming back.
Why Now?
So with the two-headed monster of Elibernaz (actually, let’s be real, it’s Albi-ass) coming back, and another Holliday offseason and/or spring training cut short due to surgery (pending wrist procedure) and him slight and brittle and unable to turn his natural speed into any kind of weapon and with him downright deficient at second base, he has to go.
With Jordan Westburg coming back from his latest surgery, and him brittle and not durable, but with a legit run-production profile this lineup desperately needs, he will be given every chance to bounce back. And at this point, I’m simplifying his program – Westburg is a second baseman. Less strain on the body there. Let’s get 120 games out of him there and some DH work.
Because we also know Elias is going to be all about Christian Encarnacion-Strand in 2027, loving to try to turn a AAAA guy into a regular, and with CES’s power productivity and the glove playing better than expected, he is in the mix. And Pete Alonso and Samuel Basallo block first base. Coby Mayo was the one young player who truly exceeded expectations on this roster, and he kills left-handed pitching and you can live with the glove at third once or twice a week.
And Gunnar Henderson is not an MLB shortstop and he won’t be here past the trade deadline and he could be dealt this winter (and they don’t have the guts to move him to third, where he’s always belonged). If he is dealt before the lockout, Blaze Alexander would be an option at short, and they should go get a glove-first shortstop anyway and stop running fake teams out there with no spine. Either way, Elias will want Alexander to play a lot, so you tell me where Holliday fits in?
What About Selling Low?
Never stopped Elias before, it’s another specialty of his, and it could always get worse. In Birdland, it always does. That's The Elias Way.
Holliday has too many voices in his head, and yet another new hitting staff that is surely on the way here as Elias scapegoats middle managers while being a 100% fraud himself, will only make it worse. I’m thinking his daddy is ready for him to have a fresh start (with a team further from alleged contention than the Orioles) and agent Scott Boras is ready for him to have a fresh start, where the pressure of being the overhyped 1-1 won’t matter as much.
We won’t belabor the point defensively, because it’s ugly all around and the instincts at 2B are not natural or fluid. He is 20th among all MLB players with at least 500 innings at second in fielding run value. He is in the 88th percentile in sprint speed and played nearly 100 games this season and had eight steals and got thrown out three times; in an era where they made stealing bases easier than ever, he has 29 steals to 14 times caught stealing for his career.
Abject failure they couldn’t fix this, but a smart organization probably can.
As for the hit tool, man, it’s still a mess. You could tell me he’ll still only be 23 by spring training, but he has 1100 MLB plate appearances and he’s also been in this org five years now and he is going backwards, rapidly. Injuries or not, he had a .640 OPS this season and he was 17 percent worse than the average MLB hitter (OPS+) … those are below his career totals (.654 OPS and 86 OPS+).
Holliday stopped swinging as hard and moved off the plate in the box and changed his swing plane in an effort to get on base more and work the ball between the gaps .. and ended up with a .300 OBP, much worse than last year, and a .229 average, also much worse than 2025. And really, the fact he ends the season on the IL like he began it, needing yet another procedure, kind of says it all.
He is a number nine hitter in a real MLB lineup, and I’m not sure where he plays most of the time. They gave him another run at the top of the lineup when he was hot in July, and that leadoff stint was largely a disaster (.267 OBP and .614 OPS). He had an amazing July, and arguably in every other month he looked like someone who needed more seasoning in AAA.
Holliday had a .582 OPS in 50 games at Camden Yards, a park that should suit him from the left side, and a .601 OPS in the second half of the season. It’s over here.
Sadly, it never even ever really got going here, and worst of all, the guy who created this problem is still the one charged with fixing it.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- The Orioles will not be heading to the 2026 postseason.
Although the O’s were off on Thursday, they were eliminated from playoff contention when the White Sox recorded a 9-1 win at Kansas City and clinched a berth for themselves. Baltimore’s odds of reaching the postseason had been low for quite some time.
With only three games remaining on the schedule (all vs. the Yankees in New York this weekend), the Orioles will look to finish strong and build positive momentum toward the offseason. And while no playoff stakes will be involved, there are still things to watch for.
Here are five things to keep an eye on during Baltimore’s final series of the season.
With only three games remaining on the schedule (all vs. the Yankees in New York this weekend), the Orioles will look to finish strong and build positive momentum toward the offseason. And while no playoff stakes will be involved, there are still things to watch for.
Here are five things to keep an eye on during Baltimore’s final series of the season.
1. Attempting to finish .500
The O’s can’t end up with a winning record, but they can still get to .500. However, they’ll need to sweep the three-game set at Yankee Stadium to make that happen, and they haven’t swept a series of three-plus games in the Bronx since June 6-8, 1986.
Baltimore is guaranteed to have a better record than it did in 2025 (75-87). It hasn’t had a year in which it finished exactly .500 since going 81-81 in 2015.
“Regardless of what the record is, I just want to play good baseball, good quality baseball, and whatever we have left in the tank, just empty the tank. Because after 162, that's it, you’ve got to wait until spring,” first baseman Pete Alonso said. “Hopefully, we win all three, because that's the goal. We want to win every game that we play, regardless of the standings.”
2. How many more homers can Alonso hit?
Through 159 games, Alonso has clubbed a team-high 41 home runs during his first season with the Orioles. And he’ll surely play all three at Yankee Stadium, as he hasn’t missed a game since the 2023 season.
Here’s the list of 41-plus-homer seasons in O’s history (since 1954):
1. Chris Davis -- 53 in 2013
2. Brady Anderson -- 50 in 1996
3. Frank Robinson -- 49 in 1966
T-4. Davis -- 47 in 2015
T-4. Mark Trumbo -- 47 in 2016
6. Jim Gentile -- 46 in 1961
7. Anthony Santander -- 44 in 2024
8. Rafael Palmeiro -- 43 in 1998
9. Alonso -- 41 in 2026
Considering Alonso has six home runs over his past eight games (including three during a three-game sweep of Toronto earlier this week), it’s possible the 31-year-old slugger will add a few more to his total, potentially passing Palmeiro and perhaps even Santander.
3. RBI history for Alonso?
Another feat that Alonso could accomplish is one no player has done before.
There’s never been an MLB player to post a pair of seasons in which he led each of the two leagues (American and National) in RBIs, since RBIs became official in 1920. Alonso led the NL with 131 RBIs in 2022, and this year, he leads the AL with 110.
4. More of The Mountain
Félix Bautista made an emotional return to the Orioles earlier this week after missing more than a year due to right shoulder surgery. The 31-year-old former All-Star closer was quite familiar with long recoveries, as he previously missed all of the 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery.
Bautista has made a pair of appearances since rejoining Baltimore’s bullpen. He allowed one run in two-thirds of an inning vs. the Brewers on Sunday, then yielded two runs in one inning against the Blue Jays on Wednesday.
The results aren’t too important at the moment, especially because Bautista hasn’t yet reassumed his closing duties. But it’s encouraging that he’s getting a few big league outings in before entering the offseason and looking to return to his previously dominant form in 2027.
“I stayed firm the entire time, focused on the hard work,” Bautista recently said via team interpreter Brandon Quinones. “I knew that it was just as long of a road [as Tommy John], and it took a lot of time. But my entire focus the entire time was just on the work itself.”
5. Trevor Rogers’ potential final O’s start
The winner of the 2025 Most Valuable Oriole Award, Rogers has been one of Baltimore’s best starters over the past two seasons. The 28-year-old left-hander has a 4.07 ERA in 29 starts, but he had some struggles early in the year. Since June 4, he has a 2.92 ERA over 19 starts.
Rogers is scheduled to start Game 2 of Friday’s doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Will it be his final time pitching for the Orioles? He is set to become a free agent after the season, but it’s possible he’ll re-sign with the club. (He could also be a prime candidate to receive a qualifying offer, which would bring him back for one more year.)

Yordan Alvarez’s great season with the Houston Astros is also generating headlines beyond his pursuit of the Triple Crown and his MVP case.
After going 2-for-4 in the Astros’ 6-5 loss to the Seattle Mariners on Wednesday, Alvarez led MLB in batting average (.314), on-base percentage (.431) and slugging percentage (.601).
The last three players to lead the Major Leagues in all three offensive percentage categories were Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (2025), and the now-retired Miguel Cabrera (2013) and Barry Bonds (2002).
The run scored by Alvarez in the third inning was the 100th of the season, to which he added 106 walks and 102 RBIs. These numbers put his season on another level, as only Judge and Bonds have been able to add at least 100 walks and 100 runs scored to their season while leading the offensive line. Entering his final three games against the Athletics, he can add to that.
Judge did it in 2025 when he led the league with 124 walks and 137 runs scored, while Bonds completed those numbers in 2002 and then again in 2004 when he walked 232 times.
An Unmatched Season in Astros History
Alvarez's season has been historic. In addition to leading the offense, he has added triple digits in runs scored, RBIs and walks, which puts his 2026 season in a historic place. No other Houston hitter has been able to achieve those three marks in a single season and, at the same time, lead the Majors in batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage.
Jeff Bagwell is the one who came closest when he led the league with 143 runs scored and 149 walks in 1999 and accumulated 42 home runs with 126 RBIs, but his .304/.454/.591 offensive line could not lead the Majors. Bagwell also had great seasons as an Astro in 1997 and 2000 without being able to reach Alvarez's impact, and something similar happened with Lance Berkman in 2002 (he led the league with 128 RBIs, scored 106 runs and took 107 walks) and Alex Bregman in 2019 (he led the league with 119 walks, drove in 112 and scored 122 runs).
Alvarez is eight RBIs away from tying Pete Alonso, who leads the American League with 110, and that could make the big difference in the race to win the Triple Crown. However, he still remains in the conversation as a solid candidate for the American League MVP award. Since Carl Yastrzemski won the American League Triple Crown in 1967, Miguel Cabrera in 2012 has been the only Triple Crown winner in the Major Leagues.
In any case, the season is not over yet and there can be excitement in these final days. That said, he will have to unleash his swing as he did throughout the season, especially before August. In that same stretch since August 1, Alonso made the difference with 18 home runs, while Alvarez has been able to hit only six.
Houston continues its four-game series against the Athletics, which could be a great opportunity for him to drive the team and continue adding historic chapters to his great season.

New York Mets fans repeatedly showed their love for Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso throughout the series between the clubs held at Citi Field earlier in September.
Following the Orioles' 4-2 win over the Toronto Blue Jays on Wednesday night, Alonso offered a quote that sparked plenty of conversations on New York sports radio station WFAN and that may annoy some Mets supporters.
"I believe in the baseball gods, and I honestly believe that, like, I'm here for a reason," Alonso said about playing for the Orioles, as shared by Avi Carr-Gloth of WMAR-2 News. "I was always meant to be a Baltimore Oriole, and I think people are very appreciative and receptive to that, and I feel just as lucky and fortunate to be here as other people have told me. So it's special. That's really an understatement."
Alonso was a homegrown Met who played only for the club from when he made his MLB debut in 2019 through the 2025 season. Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns then controversially chose not to sign the franchise's all-time home run king to a long-term contract, and Alonso ultimately inked a five-year, $155M deal to join the Orioles.
While the 73-85 Mets spent the bulk of the summer knowing they had no chance of making the playoffs, Alonso slashed .264/.359/.512 with an .871 OPS, 41 home runs and 110 RBI over his first 159 games with Baltimore en route to becoming a potential American League MVP candidate. That said, the 78-81 Orioles began Thursday knowing they likely also won't participate in the postseason tournament.
"I know this hasn’t been the season that we wanted internally, and it’s not the season that’s expected internally," Alonso added on Wednesday night, per Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner. "The people who have supported us, it’s not what they expected or wanted either. For people to still show up, come out to a doubleheader today, and really just show the true support, it’s special, and that should be recognized."
If nothing else, Alonso's latest comments won't help Stearns' popularity among the Mets fans who chanted for team owner Steve Cohen to fire the executive before and after Alonso crushed his 300th career home run in Queens on Sept. 15.

The Baltimore Orioles believed they had a shot at contending before the 2026 campaign, and have actually done it. It’s the final week, and they are still alive, even though actually making the playoffs seems almost impossible. They thought they were one big bat away, which is why they heavily pursued and signed former New York Mets slugger Pete Alonso.
Alonso, as everybody knows, has deep emotional ties to the Mets. He’s their all-time home run leader, and Citi Field showered him with love when the two teams met in a recent series. He is, however, starting to become a leader for the Orioles, both on and off the field.
On the field, Alonso has been, as expected, a beast. He entered Thursday slashing a robust .264/.359/.512 with 41 home runs, 110 RBI, and a 144 wRC+, his best mark since his incredible rookie season in 2019. His 4.7 fWAR is already tied with his highest output, also with the 2019 campaign. There's no question that he is one of the Orioles' building blocks for 2027.
The first baseman’s impact, however, is also starting to be felt in the clubhouse and the dugout. He has become a leader in the Orioles’ rebuild project, flawed as it might be. The 31-year-old slugger has been through a lot as a major leaguer and is a respected, beloved figure around the league. He knows how to deal with the highs and lows of being in the majors, and that’s someone that young Orioles players trying to establish themselves can look up to.
Meant To Be An Oriole
“I believe in the Baseball Gods, and I honestly believe I’m here for a reason. I was always meant to be a Baltimore Oriole,” Alonso said, per reporter Andy Kostka. He is grateful and genuinely happy for the opportunity to wear the Orioles uniform, and he does it with pride and dignity. He plays the game the right way.
Fans can certainly enjoy the idea of having someone who has deep respect for the franchise as a leader, even if Alonso isn’t a homegrown player. He has earned his place amongst MLB’s best players, and he chose to represent Baltimore, the city, and the O’s, the franchise.
On Wednesday, Alonso called his Orioles teammates back onto the field to salute the Baltimore crowd at Camden Yards after their final home game of the year in a really nice gesture that fans greatly appreciated. Leadership is forged in the small but meaningful details, and that definitely was one.
Alonso’s teammates followed his lead and greeted the crowd, creating a much-needed nice moment before the final few games of the season.
Even if Baltimore is eliminated on Thursday or the weekend (still the likeliest outcome even though they are still alive as of Thursday afternoon), they will enter the offseason knowing that they have a veteran figure to look up to, one that produces on the field and represents the organization with pride off it.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday afternoon, the Blue Jays were eliminated from the playoff race. The team had a disappointing season.
Naturally, this raises the question: Is this the end for Max Scherzer?
We know he's likely to make one last start on Sunday in front of the Toronto Blue Jays' fans—even if it's on short rest.
That would allow him to have a fitting farewell start in front of his fans.
We imagine he'll be looking, in particular, to surpass Justin Verlander (who will throw a few pitches on Saturday) in strikeouts.
After his seven strikeouts on Wednesday, Scherzer is four behind his former teammate with the Tigers and the Mets.
But the question on everyone's mind is this: Will Scherzer seek to return to the majors in 2027?
For now, the pitcher is keeping everyone in suspense. He'll reveal his plans in the coming days, once the season is over.
Scherzer, who has 500 career starts under his belt, was the subject of an article (in The Athletic) on Wednesday morning stating that he is aiming for a 20th season in 2027.
It's unclear whether he'll achieve that goal, but that's what he's aiming for.
In reality, it will depend on whether he feels capable of pitching and whether a team he's interested in were to make him an offer.
It's still too early to tell if the stars will align… and if his body will hold up. After all, he's realized he can no longer pitch through injuries like he did when he was younger.
Personally, I get the feeling he wants to come back. He loves baseball too much, and I think he wants more than just to narrowly surpass Justin Verlander in career strikeouts.
And above all: I also think he doesn't want to be inducted into Cooperstown at the same time as Verlander, who's retiring on Saturday. We talked about it on the podcast last night…
- The Astros lead their division with a 78-80 record.
- The Diamondbacks are still holding onto hope.
- Pete Alonso's leadership. He encouraged his teammates to tip their caps to the fans.
- Another 200-strikeout season for Chris Sale.
- Ceddanne Rafaela: Just a cramp?
- 41 home runs for Ben Rice.

Mariners rally past Astros 6-5 in 10 innings to keep faint playoff hopes alive
Posted/updated on: September 24, 2026 at 6:59 am
SEATTLE (AP) — Josh Naylor singled home Randy Arozarena with the winning run in the 10th inning and the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive by rallying past the Houston Astros 6-5 on Wednesday night.
Houston (78-80) remained tied atop the AL West with Texas, which has lost three straight games. The Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker if the teams finish with the same record.
The Mariners (74-84) are four games back with four to play.
Seattle was down 5-4 after automatic runner Yordan Alvarez scored on a triple to right field by Isaac Paredes in the top of the 10th.
With one out and the bases loaded in the bottom half, Julio Rodríguez worked a full-count walk from Astros closer Josh Hader, forcing in J.P. Crawford with the tying run. Naylor sent Hader’s next pitch to right-center, and Arozarena scored his third run of the night.
Alvarez went 2 for 4 without an RBI in his pursuit of the AL Triple Crown. That raised his league-leading batting average to .316. Tampa Bay’s Chandler Simpson, second at .309, did not play Wednesday against the New York Yankees.
Alvarez is part of a four-way tie for the home run lead at 41 with the Rays’ Junior Caminero, Baltimore’s Pete Alonso and the Yankees’ Ben Rice. The Houston slugger is second in RBIs with 102, eight behind Alonso.
Before his tying walk, Rodríguez had three hits for the Mariners.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz and Nick Allen each had two hits for Houston. One of Diaz’s hits was his 14th homer, a two-run shot to cap a four-run third.
Cooper Criswell (4-2) pitched the 10th inning to earn the win for Seattle. Hader (4-2), who also pitched the ninth, took the loss.
Seattle scored three times in the third to pull to 4-3. The first two runs came on Dominic Canzone’s double as he extended his hitting streak to a career-best 12 games. Canzone’s single in the fifth scored Arozarena to tie it at 4.
Up next
The Mariners will send right-hander Bryan Woo (12-9, 3.92 ERA) to the mound Thursday in the opener of a season-ending four-game series against the Angels.
Right-hander Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.70) will pitch for the Astros in the first game of a four-game set at the Athletics.
