item.content:encoded:
Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. They’ll recall the name Mackey Sasser for the inability to throw the ball back to the pitcher safely. Kirk Nieuwenhuis had his random 3-home run game. Luis Castillo lives on in infamy for dropping a routine pop up at Yankee Stadium to end the night.
A mix of greatness and defeat have followed the Mets since they were officially born for the 1962 MLB season. Several Hall of Famers have come through to call the Polo Grounds, Shea Stadium, and Citi Field home. Everything from a mix of the homegrown talent of Tom Seaver to the ill-fated signing of Justin Verlander have a part in Mets history.
While some players live on forever with statues or their numbers retired, so do individual seasons. Random, expected, and in other seasons a longtime coming, these 25 individual seasons by Mets players are the greatest in the franchise’s history. You can’t think of these players without recalling how impressive of a year they had.
The 25 best seasons by Mets players in franchise history
25) Gary Carter, 1985
Gary Carter’s entrance into Mets lore began with a bang. Literally. He homered on Opening Day 1985 and would continue to pummel baseballs throughout the season for his new ball club. Carter finished with a 6.9 bWAR (what does that mean in 1985?) plus 32 home runs and 100 RBI. Exactly matching the .853 OPS he had in his final year with the Montreal Expos the year prior, it was the early telltale sign the Mets made the right decision to make him a part of their core. Partly because the Mets made the playoffs the next year, Carter was able to jump from sixth to third in the MVP vote. Despite this, his 1985 season was the better one.
24) Cleon Jones, 1969
Offense isn’t what won the Mets the 1969 World Series. The hitting was okay, but for the longest time, Cleon Jones’ .340 batting average sat well above anyone else in franchise history. Worth 7 bWAR in part because of an atypical season where he actually rated positively as a defender, Jones had an often-overlooked year where he finished 7th in the NL MVP vote. In an era when pitching dominated, Jones’ season deserves more credit. The year might not compare as well as some Mets years with 30+ home runs or 100+. However, for the timing of when it took place and the well-aged batting average, Jones deserves the accolades.
23) Jesse Orosco, 1983
Spoiler alert! There won’t be another relief pitcher on this list. They’re sometimes hard to judge because of how many fewer innings they throw. Plus, with the ever-evolving usage of arms, they don’t stack up well against each other in different eras. Nevertheless, what Jesse Orosco accomplished in 1983 was outlandish. At 13-7 all out of the bullpen, he tossed 110 innings and had a 1.47 ERA. The effort earned him third place in the NL Cy Young. It was a one-of-a-kind type of season from a Mets reliever. Somewhat unspoken, it was only his second full season as a major league pitcher and already he was at the top of his game while helping to further define the closer role.
22) Jose Reyes, 2006
Several different Jose Reyes seasons deserve to be on this list. How does one differentiate between them? He won a batting title in 2011 but lacked in other areas. In 2006, he hit .300, had a career-best 5.9 bWAR, and stole 64 bases. Most memorable was scoring 122 runs and driving in another 81. Homering 19 times helped make this maybe his most prolific offensive season for New York. The 2006 Mets are remembered for their incredible lineup. Reyes at the very top was one of the biggest factors.
21) Edgardo Alfonzo, 2000
Edgardo Alfonzo is a beloved Mets player. He crosses off a lot of the boxes fans desire. He was homegrown, versatile, and put together some really good years for winning ball clubs. In 2000, he wasn’t the main attraction and yet the season’s totals hold up nicely all of these years later. His lone All-Star season included a career-best 6.4 bWAR with 25 home runs and 94 RBI. Both of those numbers were a little short of what he did the year previous. However, his .967 OPS overpowered any of his past seasons and remains one of the best in Mets history. Alfonzo could be trusted to hit anywhere from first to fifth in the lineup if needed.
20) Lance Johnson, 1996
The 1996 Mets weren’t very good, but they did have three players who hit really well. One of the trio put together a season that landed him on the record books and doesn’t look like it’ll be surpassed. Lance Johnson’s 227 hits and 21 triples both set single-season Mets records while leading the league. In addition to the bat, he stole 50 bases and earned himself a 1.9 dWAR. If we were ranking only seasons by Mets leadoff hitters, this would be right near the top. It’s a shame this couldn’t have occurred on a better season for the team.
19) Jerry Koosman, 1968
Jerry Koosman did something amazing. By many measurements, his best year was his first. Koosman had a small sampling in the majors during the 1967 season. The following year qualified as his rookie campaign. Koosman went 19-12 with a 2.08 ERA. He’d end up 13th in the Cy Young race and the runner-up for the Rookie of the Year, just barely, when Johnny Bench beat him for the honor. A coin toss might have been the decider for some voters as both NL rookies had a case. Koosman was later the Cy Young runner-up in 1976. Compared to 1968, his freshman year was the better of the two.
18) David Cone, 1988
Who says wins don’t matter? In 1988, David Cone went a remarkable 20-3. He wasn’t vulturing wins thanks to the help of a strong offense. Cone pitched to a 2.22 ERA while finishing third in the Cy Young race and 10th in the MVP vote. A somewhat underrated pitcher whose career spanned the lighter hitting 1980s through the Steroid Era of the 1990s, this first full season in a Mets uniform was a preview of the strikeout machine he’d later become. Fanning 212, he’d later manage to lead the league in 1990 and 1991. The ERA in 1988 was about a full run better making this the more worthy campaign.
17) Pete Alonso, 2019
Pete Alonso posted some of the most unique statistics in Mets history. The power is unmatched in a single season and career. His rookie season in 2019 featuring 53 home runs and 120 RBI also included a 5.4 bWAR and a career-high .941 OPS. The record-setting debut season out of Alonso was more than enough to make a lasting impression on Mets fans who will never stop loving him. Alonso, like some others on this list, gets bonus points for doing it as a rookie. Those 53 home runs will be tough for a veteran, let alone a player with no MLB experience, to ever match. He became the Mets home run king for a reason. His power is unmatched from just the eye test.
16) Juan Soto, 2025
Statistically impressive, the only thing missing from Juan Soto’s first year with the Mets was purpose. The team collapsed late despite Soto putting together yet another one of his token MVP-caliber seasons. Along with hitting 43 home runs and posting a league-high .396 OBP, Soto stole 38 bases. His previous single-season high was 12. Truly a one-of-a-kind type of year, the only reason this isn’t higher is because the defense slowed him down. It was the type of year to build off of while making his record-setting contract worth it to Steve Cohen.
15) Francisco Lindor, 2024
Francisco Lindor’s MVP runner-up season in 2024 needs to be experienced to fully understand. He started off as poorly as the team and managed to quite literally lead the club to the NLCS. His first 30/30 season which includes his time in Cleveland was far more complicated than just looking at the .844 OPS. Lindor was a leader and with another Gold Glove-caliber season at shortstop, managed to put together a 6.8 bWAR season. Nothing about the season was statistically insane yet Lindor seemed to do a little bit of everything well.
14) Darryl Strawberry, 1987
Strangely, the best season of Darryl Strawberry’s career with the Mets took place in a non-playoff campaign. The 1987 Mets were good, but not good enough. Strawberry set new career highs with 39 home runs and 104 RBI. Slashing .284/.398/.583 with 36 stolen bases, it was maybe the most complete year Strawberry had as an offensive player. Although he’d lead the league in multiple offensive categories in 1988, many of his 1987 totals were superior. Crossing 30 home runs and 100 RBI for the first time in his career, it was a bit of a transition from Strawberry being one of the star players to be the signature member of the Mets.
13) Bernard Gilkey, 1996
Mets fans who weren’t familiar with Bernard Gilkey’s work might assume he was always one of the better middle of the order hitters. Arriving via trade with the St. Louis Cardinals prior to the 1996 season, Gilkey cranked it up to a whole new level. It feels appropriate that he’d later make a cameo in Men in Black because Gilkey’s numbers were unworldly. He slashed .317/.393/.562 with 44 doubles, 30 home runs, and 117 RBI. The doubles are still the most of any Mets player in a single-season. The 8.1 bWAR became the best in Mets history by a position player. Created by both his bat and glove, Gilkey led the league with 18 assists, 4 double plays, 309 putouts, and ranked as the best at his position in range factor.
12) Tom Seaver, 1975
You knew Tom Seaver was coming eventually. His 1975 season earned him his third and final Cy Young Award. He probably could have had more. This season was a 7.8 bWAR campaign that had him going 22-9 with a 2.38 ERA and a league-leading 243 strikeouts. Compared to most players, it’s incredible. On the list of Seaver performances, this one is easy to overlook because even one of his non-Cy Young winning years was better. Don’t worry. Tom Terrific is all over this list with several seasons that were even better.
11) Tom Seaver, 1969
When it comes to Mets greatness, Tom Seaver is the “you haven’t seen the last of me!” in franchise history. The 1969 season ended with a championship for the Mets. In the regular season, Seaver won a franchise-record 25 games while on his way to his first Cy Young and an MVP runner-up. Neither the 2.21 ERA nor 208 strikeouts would set personal bests. This might have been the most rewarding individual season of Seaver’s career yet it falls short of his best by quite a couple. At least he got winning the big one out of the way relatively early.
10) Jacob deGrom, 2019
Speaking of Cy Young Mets seasons, Jacob deGrom got his second in 2019. His 7.2 bWAR led the league as did the 255 strikeouts. By this point, greatness was something Mets fans weren’t demanding from deGrom, it was expected. A good length away from some of those other memorable Mets seasons by pitchers like Tom Seaver, his 2.43 ERA doesn’t even do him justice for how dominant he was for his second straight season as the best pitcher in the sport. Sadly, this would end up as his final full season in a Mets uniform due to a pandemic as well as injuries in 2021 and 2022.
9) Mike Piazza, 2000
Mike Piazza had big years, moments, and numbers with the Mets. Because his defense behind the plate was never good, stats like WAR don’t rank quite as high as some others. The 2000 season was big regardless as Piazza hit .324/.398/.614 with a 1.012 OPS. The OPS was the largest in any full season for a Mets player. The year included 38 home runs and 113 RBI with the real kicker being that he had only 482 at-bats. One of those more underrated qualities about his offensive abilities, he walked 58 times while only going down on strikes 69 times.
8) Howard Johnson, 1989
Howard Johnson led the league in home runs and RBI in 1991, but it was his 1989 season which deserves a spot on this list. Armed with 36 home runs and 101 RBI, Johnson’s speed went on display with 41 stolen bases. It was his second 30/30 season with the Mets. He hit .287 as well, atypical for the .251 he hit while in orange and blue. Never the biggest star on the Mets roster during his best years in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Johnson’s powerful and speedy 1989 campaign was a special one and the best representation of what he had to offer the ball club during his peak seasons.
7) John Olerud, 1998
Each of the three seasons John Olerud spent with the Mets was special in its own way. A franchise-leading .354 batting average helps break the tie. That’s what he hit in 1998, his middle season with the club. Posting a 7.6 bWAR as well, Olerud was the 12th place finisher in the MVP race during a season where you didn’t get much attention if you weren’t hitting home runs. He had 22 with 93 RBI. More like Keith Hernandez leveled up on offense, newer statistics that emphasis on base have helped this season age better. Olerud was never the best first baseman in the league. In Mets history, he’s right there as one of the stronger overall performers.
6) Carlos Beltran, 2006
Carlos Beltran overcame a rough first year with the Mets in 2005 to put together one of the all-time great ones in 2006. The 41 home runs hit by Todd Hundley in 1996 were matched by Beltran. Posting an 8.2 bWAR, he set a new single-season high in franchise history that would only get to enjoy one season at the top. Beltran slashed .275/.388/.594. He had 95 walks and only 99 strikeouts to practically cancel each other out. The only negative about his season was how it ended. The visual of striking out looking to end Game 7 of the NLCS remains one of the first fans often think about when his name or heartbreaking Mets moments are mentioned.
5) David Wright, 2007
No Mets player has ever matched the popularity of David Wright. His 2007 season, an 8.3 bWAR campaign, set a new mark of excellence. This was Captain America at his absolute best. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, and cruised past 100 runs scored and RBI. He even hit .325 with a .416 OBP. To make sure no check boxes were left unfilled, he won a Silver Slugger and Gold Glove. The team’s collapse in 2007 likely had to do a lot with why he only finished fourth in the MVP.
4) Jacob deGrom, 2018
As much as Jacob deGrom’s ridiculously good 15-start season in 2021 was historic, it wasn’t a complete year. The 2018 season, on the other hand, included 32 starts and a magnificent 1.70 ERA. This was deGrom’s true coming out party. The debate all year was whether or not a pitcher with a losing record could win the Cy Young. He finished at 10-9 to void the conversation and was one vote shy of a unanimous decision for his first time winning the award. The season included multiple highs for deGrom including 269 strikeouts. It was the ultimate one-man army type of season in Mets history where the team was, oftentimes, only worth watching every fifth day.
3) Tom Seaver, 1971
Here’s the most ridiculous detail about the 1971 season for Tom Seaver: he didn’t win the Cy Young. A league-leading 10.2 bWAR wouldn’t have been known at the time, but a 20-10 record and league-best 1.76 ERA as well as 289 strikeouts to overtake every other pitcher in the National League should have been enough. Seaver settled as the runner-up to Ferguson Jenkins who had a 2.77 ERA and a 24-13 record. The race wasn’t even all that close with Jenkins getting 17 first-place votes and Seaver receiving 6. Both the Mets and Chicago Cubs won 83 games so it’s not as if team record mattered at all. In practically any other year, Seaver would have added more hardware to his collection.
2) Tom Seaver, 1973
If you crave Tom Seaver content, you’re in the right place. His 1973 season earned him his second Cy Young. He had a career-best 10.6 bWAR featuring a league-high 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games, and 251 strikeouts. The Mets would sneak into the postseason and then overtake the Big Red Machine Cincinnati Reds on their way to the World Series. The Mets fell short, of course, but the regular season showing by Seaver was valuable at cementing his Hall of Fame legacy. We can even include the playoffs if there was any doubt. Although he was 1-2 overall, he pitched to a 1.62 ERA in the NLCS and had a 2.40 ERA in the World Series. All the Mets were missing was league-average offense to win another championship.
1) Dwight Gooden, 1985
There shouldn’t have been any question as to what the best season by a Mets player was going to be because what Dwight Gooden did in 1985 was one of the greatest in MLB history. The 12.2 bWAR ranks as the 26th best in MLB history. It’s the best after 1913. Gooden went 24-4 with a 1.53 ERA. He led the league in complete games, innings, and struck out 268 batters. Those numbers matter a lot, as does one other one. Gooden was only 20-years-old for the entire season. This is the kind of year that’ll go unmatched by a Mets player until some sort of cosmic shift in the way the game is played or with the rule book. You can safely etch this into stone as the best.
Hall of Famers, players with retired numbers, some completely random yet memorable performances, and even a few active members cracked the list of the best individual Mets player seasons. Records were broken. Memories were made. In a couple of cases, championships were won.

Josh Naylor's walk-off single in 10th propels Mariners past Astros
(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive with a 6-5 victory against the visiting Houston Astros on Wednesday night.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners (74-84), whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston (78-80) and Texas (78-80), who are tied atop the American League West.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier hitting a two-run homer for the Astros.
Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2), who pitched the ninth, returned to the mound in the 10th to try and put the Astros into sole possession of the division lead. With J.P. Crawford the automatic runner, Hader walked Randy Arozarena before Canzone hit a slow roller to shortstop Nick Allen to advance both runners. A walk to Cal Raleigh loaded the bases and another to Julio Rodriguez forced in the tying run. Naylor lined the first pitch he saw from Hader up the middle to win it.
Mariners reliever Cooper Criswell (4-2) allowed one run on one hit with one strikeout in one inning.
The Astros opened the scoring with four runs in the top of the third off Mariners starter George Kirby. With one out, Allen doubled to left. Jose Altuve hit what turned out to be a single down the left-field line that deflected off third-base umpire Ryan Blakney's shin. Yordan Alvarez doubled to right, sending Altuve to third, before Isaac Paredes lifted a sacrifice fly to right. Diaz then lined a two-run shot over the left-field wall to make it 4-0.
The Mariners responded with three runs in the bottom of the inning against Astros starter Ethan Pecko. Lazaro Montes drew a leadoff walk and, an out later, Crawford grounded a single to right. Both runners advanced on a wild pitch. Arozarena walked to load the bases for Canzone, who lined a two-run single off the right-field wall. With two outs, Rodriguez lined a double to left to cut Houston's lead to 4-3.
The Mariners tied it in the fifth off reliever Josh Hendrickson, who was making his MLB debut. Arozarena lined a one-out single to center, stole second and scored on Canzone's single to center.
Pecko pitched 2 2/3 innings and gave up three runs on four hits. The rookie right-hander walked two and struck out two.
Kirby went five innings and allowed four runs on six hits. The right-hander walked three and fanned five.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
El lanzador de los Atlanta Braves alcanzó una cifra histórica y reafirmó su dominio desde la lomita a sus 37 años
Chris Sale volvió a colocar su nombre entre los grandes lanzadores de las Grandes Ligas. El zurdo de los Atlanta Braves alcanzó la cifra de 200 ponches en una temporada por novena ocasión en su carrera, un registro que lo coloca dentro de un grupo exclusivo en la historia reciente de MLB.
El serpentinero consiguió la marca al ponchar a 10 bateadores durante la victoria de este miércoles 23 de septiembre por walk-off de los Bravos por 3-2 ante los Cincinnati Reds en el Truist Parkla y reafirmó una de las características que han definido su trayectoria: su capacidad para dominar a los bateadores mediante la potencia de su recta, su slider y una mecánica que durante años lo convirtió en uno de los lanzadores más difíciles de enfrentar.
Además, Sale se unió a Randy Johnson como los únicos lanzadores zurdos en la historia de MLB con nueve o más campañas superando los 200 ponches. La lista de pitchers con más temporadas de este tipo está encabezada por Nolan Ryan, con 15, seguido por Randy Johnson, con 13, Roger Clemens, con 12, y Tom Seaver, con 10.
Además de su cifra de ponches, el veterano cerró la temporada regular con una efectividad de 2.16, uno de los mejores registros entre los lanzadores calificados de MLB. Solamente Jacob Misiorowski (1.86) y Cam Schlittler (1.94) presentan mejores números entre quienes cumplen con los requisitos estadísticos.
Su campaña también lo coloca dentro de la historia de los Braves. Desde 1920, únicamente Greg Maddux —con efectividades de 1.56 en 1994 y 1.63 en 1995—, Reynaldo López —1.99 en 2024— y Warren Spahn —2.10 en 1953— habían registrado una efectividad de 2.16 o menor en al menos 25 aperturas durante una temporada con la franquicia.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Pete Alonso busca una marca histórica que nadie ha conseguido en 106 años de Grandes Ligas
Chris Sale vuelve a alcanzar una cifra histórica
La temporada con 200 ponches representa un nuevo capítulo en la carrera de Sale, quien alcanzó esta cifra por primera vez en 2012, cuando todavía pertenecía a los Chicago White Sox.
Desde entonces, el lanzador mantuvo una notable regularidad como especialista en ponchar rivales. Sus registros le permitieron superar nuevamente la barrera de los 200 abanicados en múltiples campañas con los White Sox, Boston Red Sox y ahora Atlanta Braves.
La marca confirma la trayectoria de un pitcher que ha enfrentado diferentes etapas dentro de MLB, incluidos periodos marcados por lesiones, pero que logró mantenerse como una referencia cuando estuvo disponible sobre la lomita.
Un dominio que se mantiene con el paso de los años
Chris Sale ha construido su reputación sobre su capacidad para generar swings fallidos y limitar la producción ofensiva de sus rivales. A lo largo de su carrera se ha caracterizado por mantener altos niveles de ponches y una presencia constante entre los lanzadores más destacados de la liga.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Alex Bregman recibe pelotazo en el rostro y abandona juego de Cubs
El zurdo explicó la importancia de mantenerse enfocado durante una temporada larga y destacó el trabajo colectivo detrás de sus resultados. “No lo haces solo. Es un esfuerzo de todos los días, de preparación, de trabajo y de tener la confianza de tus compañeros”, señaló Sale sobre el camino que lo llevó nuevamente a alcanzar una cifra histórica.
Su consistencia también le permitió sumar reconocimientos individuales, como el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional en 2024, además de múltiples apariciones en el Juego de Estrellas.
Sale mantiene la potencia de su brazo rumbo a los playoffs
Más allá de los números, Sale demostró que su velocidad y capacidad de dominio siguen vigentes. En su última apertura de temporada regular, su recta de cuatro costuras alcanzó un promedio de 97.8 millas por hora, una de sus mejores marcas con ese lanzamiento como abridor desde 2018. Además, realizó cuatro lanzamientos que superaron las 99.5 millas por hora, una muestra de que su brazo mantiene la potencia pese al paso de los años.
El siguiente reto para Sale será la postemporada. El lanzador está programado para abrir el primer juego de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Nacional ante los Padres, donde buscará trasladar su dominio de la temporada regular al escenario más importante de MLB.
A sus 37 años, Chris Sale continúa agregando capítulos a una carrera marcada por los ponches, los reconocimientos individuales y ahora una nueva marca histórica que lo coloca junto a algunos de los mejores lanzadores zurdos en la historia de las Grandes Ligas.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox move Sunday's game and will play doubleheader against Cubs on Friday with storm expected
CHICAGO -- Major League Baseball's postseason is rapidly approaching.
The Chicago Cubs and White Sox are among teams who had a chance to clinch a playoff spot Wednesday evening, but they both lost their games.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are seeking a third straight World Series title. It remains to be seen how much some of the game's biggest stars will be able to participate in the playoffs, though.
The Dodgers are once again among the best teams in the big leagues, and they'll have several challengers in October, including the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. All three teams could finish the regular season with 100 wins or more. Los Angeles is rolling into the postseason and four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani is expected to return to the lineup on Wednesday after a stint on the injured list.
The New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox and Atlanta Braves have also clinched spots in the postseason. Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, a three-time AL MVP, is dealing with a right calf strain that will likely keep him out through at least the Wild Card Series.
While the 12-team playoff field appears mostly set, there are a few long-shot contenders for the postseason, and specific matchups are in flux.
Here's some of what to watch as the season comes to a close.
Here's who can clinch a playoff spot Wednesday
In the American League, the Cleveland Guardians can qualify for the postseason with a win at Boston and a loss by either the Texas Rangers or Houston Astros.
The Chicago White Sox can cap a turnaround season and earn a spot in October with a win over the Kansas City Royals and a loss by the Rangers.
Over in the National League, the Chicago Cubs can clinch a playoff spot with a win over the Miami Marlins or a loss by the Arizona Diamondbacks. The Philadelphia Phillies can clinch a wild card if they beat the Milwaukee Brewers and either the San Diego Padres or D-backs lose.
The Padres can clinch a playoff spot with a win over the Dodgers and a loss by the D-backs.
AL Central and West are tight, other division winners are set
There's quite a bit of mediocrity in the AL Central and West divisions this season, which has led to some fascinating pennant races and could lead to a sub-.500 team making the postseason.
The Guardians (82-75) have a narrow advantage over the White Sox (81-76) in the AL Central while the Texas Rangers (78-79) and Astros (78-79) are fighting for the AL West.
Over in the National League, the playoff bracket is close to set.
The Cubs (87-70), Padres (87-70) and Phillies (87-70) are jockeying for position in the wild-card race but will almost certainly make the postseason. The only team within shouting distance is Arizona (83-74), which is four games back. Chicago holds the head-to-head tiebreaker for home field over Philadelphia and San Diego, and the Phillies own the tiebreaker over the Padres after sweeping that season series 6-0.
MLB's major awards probably won't have much drama this season.
Both MVP races have strong favorites with Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong running away with the NL honor while Houston's Yordan Alvarez is the probable choice in the AL, though Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero has also had a fantastic season. Alvarez still has an outside shot at a Triple Crown. He leads the AL in batting average at .314 and his 41 homers are tied with Caminero, but his 102 RBIs are six back of Baltimore's Pete Alonso.
For the Cy Young Award, Milwaukee flame thrower Jacob Misiorowski and New York ace Cam Schlittler are the favorites in the NL and AL, respectively.
The Rookie of the Year races also look set with Cincinnati's Sal Stewart and his 110-RBI season the leader in the NL and Detroit's Kevin McGonigle the favorite in the AL.
There are 12 teams that qualify for MLB's postseason, including six teams from both the AL and NL. The three division winners in each league get seeds No. 1 through No. 3, ranked by win-loss record. Then the three wild-card teams get seeds No. 4 through No. 6, also ranked by win-loss record.
The top two teams with the best record in both the AL and NL automatically advance to the Division Series. The other eight teams play in the Wild Card Series, which is a best-of-three format beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 29. In both the AL and NL, the No. 6 seed will travel to face the No. 3 seed while the No. 5 seed goes to No. 4. The higher seed hosts all three games.
The winners then advance to the best-of-five Division Series, followed by the best-of-seven League Championship Series and a best-of-seven World Series between the winners of the AL and NL.
Wild Card Series: Sept. 29-Oct. 1 (NBC/Peacock)
Division Series: Oct. 3-10 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
Championship Series: Oct. 11-20 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
World Series: Oct. 23-31 (FOX)
The Dodgers (+220) are the favorites to capture a third straight World Series title while the Brewers (+600), Yankees (+800) and Rays (+800) are viewed as the top contenders.
The Red Sox are adjusting the schedule of their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs because of a significant storm that's expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to the Boston area.
The team said it was moving the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. The first game is scheduled to begin at 1:05 p.m. EST. The originally scheduled 7:05 p.m. EST night game was moved up to 6:05.
The Red Sox said in a press release Wednesday that the change was made in consultation with Major League Baseball.
The Cubs are currently in a tight race for one of the NL's three wild-card spots.
There was no mention of a change to Saturday's game, which is slated for a 7:15 p.m. EST first pitch.
ABC7 Chicago contributed to this report.

They were two outs away from winning the World Series. Two, measly, outs. Instead, they lost one of the most heartbreaking Game 7's in baseball history and they won't even get a shot at redemption in 2026. The Toronto Blue Jays were officially eliminated from playoff contention on Wednesday afternoon (Sept. 23) after losing a 4-2 ball game to the Orioles in Baltimore.
Like much of the season, the Blue Jays offense was painful to watch. They managed ten hits against Baltimore pitching, but went 1-for-14 with Runners in Scoring Position. 42-year-old future Hall of Famer Max Scherzer battled valiantly over five innings, but gave up four runs on four hits and three walks while striking out seven.
One of the big differences? The Orioles hit a two-run home run in the fifth off the bat of Pete Alonso. It was one of just five hits in the ball game for Baltimore. Out of Toronto's ten hits, four of them went for extra bases, all doubles, but without the ability to get a ball to leave the yard, the Blue Jays were left empty handed once the Nathan Lukes struck out to end the ball game.
Blue Jays ugly habit of not cashing in prevails once again as team is officially eliminated from playoff contention
That was the fitting frustration of the afternoon, and really, of the entire season. The Blue Jays had plenty of opportunities, but once again failed to turn them into crooked numbers that could change a game. Ten hits should be enough to put real pressure on an opponent, especially with the season on the line. Instead, Toronto kept finding ways to leave runners stranded.
With runners in scoring position this season, the Blue Jays produced a 92 wRC+, which ranked 28th in MLB, along with a .313 on-base percentage that ranked 29th. For a team that spent parts of the summer trying to convince itself there was still a path back into the postseason picture, that simply was not good enough. The lack of finishing power was just as damaging. Toronto hit only 34 home runs with runners in scoring position, tied for 27th in the league.
Of the Blue Jays’ 149 home runs this season, 84 came with nobody on base, and their overall home run total ranked dead last in baseball, tied with the LA Angels and the Milwaukee Brewers. The Brewers are playoff bound and might just be one of the World Series favourites and they found a way to score with limited power - something the Blue Jays did not. In fact, the Brewers have scored 806 runs, which is the second most in MLB.
On the day their playoff hopes officially disappeared, the Blue Jays never got the big swing the needed - a microcosm of their season long issues.
The season is technically not over. The Blue Jays still have more baseball to play later today (Sept. 23) as they are set to finish the second game of this day-night doubleheader. Then they will head home to play the Cincinnati Reds for three more games. What will follow is one of the longest winters in recent Blue Jays memory where the Blue Jays’ front office will have to go back to the drawing board to figure out what didn’t work and how to correct it before 2027.

After Carlos Rodón took care of the Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday afternoon, I tweeted that the Yankees had locked in homefield in the Wild Card Series and, with it, guaranteed they would not go to Fenway Park this postseason. I spoke slightly too soon.
The Yankees are officially cemented as the AL's No. 4 seed; that won't change, after the Rays took care of business in the nightcap and ended any faint AL East title hopes. But while the Boston Red Sox remain overwhelmingly likely to be headed to Yankee Stadium next week, their struggles down the stretch have opened a very strange door. Given the respective schedules of the Red Sox, White Sox, and Guardians, you can almost see a world where Boston has to head to the other side of the bracket instead.
We're not telling you what and what not to root for, but it's always fun to see Boston lose and struggle to harness their momentum ahead of an October run. If the Guardians handle business at Fenway, then struggle against a Royals team that wants to play spoiler, all the White Sox have to do is take care of KC and the Rockies. The Red Sox's sloppy final series with the Cubs, that may end up rescheduled and weather-addled, could factor into this calculus, too.
Red Sox could sneak into an easier path and avoid the Yankees until theoretical ALCS
Of course, don't get too excited; if this were to happen, the Red Sox would face borderline-.500 teams in the Astros/Rangers to kick off their playoff run, followed by a tilt with the AL Central winner. They'd have an easier shot at the ALCS that way, avoiding the Yankees/Rays until the best-of-seven. That may actually be what they'd want.
All of this to say: What happened to the beautiful world we used to live in in the 1990s/2000s where there was only one Wild Card and division rivals couldn't face each other before the ALCS? We should be sitting back with a bowl of popcorn laughing at the Red Sox falling short after their summer surge and gearing up for a Yankees-Guardians ALDS. Instead, MLB decided to embrace the NFL model and let sub-.500 loser teams into the big dance. Shame.
The Yankees' final five games are now officially meaningless, unless you like watching exhibition baseball and crossing your fingers that nobody slips on wet grass. While unlikely, this potential seeding swap at least gives us something to watch for (other than some Pete Alonso porch jobs and a Josh Hart bobblehead during the final weekend).

BALTIMORE — Wednesday afternoon's game between the Toronto Blue Jays and Baltimore Orioles at Oriole Park at Camden Yards had more of a spring training environment than two teams battling to stay alive in the American League postseason race deserved.
A postponement of Tuesday night's clash between the AL East rivals forced a split doubleheader on Wednesday, and the sparse crowd of 10,562 in Baltimore reflected the reality of a Wednesday matinee.
However, those in attendance were treated to more history from Pete Alonso in what has been a magical season in Charm City.
Alonso smashed a two-run homer, his 41st of the season, to pace Baltimore to a 4-2 win and stay alive for the postseason. His home run off Toronto's Max Scherzer pushed Alonso into a tie for first in the AL with Houston's Yordan Alvarez and Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero. He also ended the afternoon as the AL's leader in RBI with 110.
Pete Alonso extends the @Orioles lead with a 2-run shot ❄️ pic.twitter.com/4gBdpOtdDu
— MLB (@MLB) September 23, 2026
All of those stats and all of the things that Alonso has meant to the Orioles this season makes the veteran first baseman a strong candidate for the AL Most Valuable Player Award, said teammate Chris Bassitt.
"Pete deserves MVP votes, and he deserves them every single year. That's just the reality," Bassitt said after earning his ninth victory of the season on Wednesday afternoon. "He's one of the most underappreciated players in our game. He's easily in the top three hitters every single year."
Each of Alonso's last six hits have been home runs, becoming the first Oriole to accomplish that since Mark Trumbo hit seven home runs between Aug. 11-22, 2016.
"He's not having a crazy historical year for his standards. It's just Pete being Pete," Bassitt said. "I think Pete has held the standard of what he's done for years, and I think people are not only realizing 'Holy s--t, this guy's really good' but that he's always been really, really good."

BALTIMORE -- After being named the unanimous winner of the 2026 Most Valuable Oriole Award on Wednesday morning, Pete Alonso took the field at Camden Yards and continued what is shaping up to be an incredible finish to his first year in Baltimore.
Alonso belted his 41st home run of the season to lift the Orioles to a 4-2 victory over the Blue Jays in Game 1 of a split doubleheader. It marked the Polar Bear’s third homer over the first two games of this American League East rivalry series, as he swatted a pair in Monday night’s 4-3 comeback win.
It also helped the O’s stay alive in the AL Wild Card race for at least a bit longer. With an elimination number of one, Baltimore would be eliminated with either a loss in Game 2 of the twin bill against Toronto or via a White Sox win at Kansas City.
Although the Orioles may not end up in the playoffs, they continue to feel great about what Alonso has brought to the club -- and what the 31-year-old slugger should bring throughout the remainder of the five-year, $155 million contract he signed this past December.
Alonso is one of only eight players to hit 41 or more homers in a season in O’s history (since 1954), posting the ninth such campaign overall. His AL-high 110 RBIs are the most by a Baltimore player since Chris Davis had 117 in 2015.
The only AL players with as many homers as Alonso this season are Houston’s Yordan Alvarez and Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, who each entered Wednesday with 41.
With nine home runs over his past 18 games (and 18 homers in 41 games since Aug. 9), Alonso is continuing to climb the Orioles’ all-time single-season home run leaderboard. Next on the list is Rafael Palmeiro, who hit 43 in 1998.
Alonso, who has started every game this season, has four more games to add to his homer total -- Wednesday’s nightcap vs. the Blue Jays, followed by a three-game set against the Yankees in New York this weekend.
Despite the large contract and even larger expectations, Alonso said he hasn’t felt any added pressure to perform in 2026.
“It’s not trying to be anything different or anything more or less than who I am and what I can bring on a day-to-day basis,” Alonso said. “There’s a lot of comfort and peace of mind in that, where it’s like, ‘Hey, we believe in you, not just from a player’s side, but what you bring as a personality and teammate.’ For me, that speaks volumes.
“For me, it’s just justification. It’s like, ‘Hey, who you are, we need that, and we appreciate what you do.’ And they’re just like, ‘Go be yourself.’ What that entails is just being the best you can on the field between the lines and the best teammate you can be every single day. I really appreciate the runway, obviously.”
All season, Alonso’s leadership has drawn as much praise as his on-field performance.
“The biggest thing that stands out with Pete is, yeah, he’s going out there and competing, he wants to go out there and produce for the team, but he also wants everyone around him to do the same thing,” manager Craig Albernaz said. “He wants to help. He wants to pull everyone in the right direction, for the team and to win games.”
Alonso’s two-run blast in the fifth inning in Wednesday’s opener was his first off veteran right-hander Max Scherzer, his Mets teammate during the 2022 and ‘23 seasons. Alonso was previously 4-for-25 (.160) with two doubles, one walk and 12 strikeouts lifetime vs. Scherzer.
Right-hander Chris Bassitt turned in another solid outing, allowing two earned runs over five-plus innings. Although the 37-year-old had a 4.59 ERA in 20 games (18 starts), he recorded a 3.74 ERA over his final eight outings after returning from a back injury in mid-August.
Bassitt, who was also teammates with Alonso in New York in 2022, hasn’t been surprised at all by Alonso’s performance this season.
“Pete deserves MVP votes, and he deserves them every single year. That’s just the reality. He’s one of the most underappreciated players in our game. He’s easily a top three hitter every single year,” Bassitt said. “He’s not having a crazy historical year for his standards. It’s just Pete being Pete, and people are like, ‘Dang, this is really, really special.’ But he’s been doing that for years.
“Pete just held the standard of what he’s done for years, and I think people are now realizing, ‘Holy [crap], this guy’s really good.’ But he’s always been really, really good. So yeah, it’s Pete being Pete.”

For a lot of the season, there has seemed to be only one obvious choice to end up as the Most Valuable Oriole. You never know if some voters will talk themselves into something silly to stop it from being unanimous. In 2026, it was so obvious that even those people got it right. Pete Alonso was announced ahead of Wednesday's doubleheader as the Most Valuable Oriole for this season.
The only real downer about Alonso's first season as an Oriole is the fact that so much of the roster around him was incapable for large stretches of the season of doing its part to make this a good Orioles team. Alonso's 40 homers, .265/.359/.510 batting line, and 4.6 bWAR (hopefully with more to come over the last five games) were, in some sense, "wasted." The team will probably be eliminated from postseason contention officially today.
That doesn't take entirely away from the joy that Alonso has brought to the Orioles. He's also brought better-than-advertised first base defense. If he doesn't win a Gold Glove, that would be an egregious snub. He seems excited to be an Oriole in a way that comes along maybe once or twice in a decade, and his sign-off of every interview with "Let's go O's" is charming. We can all feel good about that contract going for four more years, at least for now.
The unanimous selection of Alonso marked the first time that the team had a unanimous winner since Cedric Mullins was the choice in 2021. That was the year that Mullins had the 30 home run/30 stolen base season for the Orioles, breaking out at the plate after giving up on being a switch hitter.
The Orioles do not announce the exact vote breakdown, or even who votes for this award. It is a mystery list of media and broadcasters who cover the team. Camden Chat is not included on that list. Ballots are submitted with a first place, second place, and third place, and the winner is tallied based on a points system. It's easy when it's unanimous for first place.
What the Orioles do announce is a list of players who did not win but also received votes. These guys were all on at least one voter's ballot, in addition to the unanimous winner, Alonso: Blaze Alexander, Samuel Basallo, Shane Baz, Kyle Bradish, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Rico Garcia, Gunnar Henderson, Trevor Rogers, and Brandon Young.
Weird votes are typically a fixture of this opaque process. Last year was a bigger "weird vote" year – somebody actually voted for interim manager Tony Mansolino a year ago. Somebody else, or maybe the same person, voted for Dylan Carlson, who was a -0.7 bWAR player for the 2025 Orioles. Most of these guys on the 2026 list were at least good for part of the season and can be somewhat justified as choices. Nobody voted for Craig Albernaz or this year's negative bWAR outfielders, Dylan Beavers and Leody Taveras.
In the case of Alexander and Encarnacion-Strand, they just didn't get to play enough to demonstrate more value; their overall performance was good in the games that they played. Alexander missed a bunch of games due to getting bones broken by a hit by pitch. Encarnacion-Strand only arrived in the organization during the season. He might turn out to be a Ryan O'Hearn kind of late bloomer story, or he might turn out to be a Jeremiah Jackson kind of flash in the plan.
When it comes to guys like Bradish, Henderson, Rogers, and Mayo, they weren't good for significant portions of the season, so their season numbers don't look like anything special. You have to squint more for some than for others to see the case. Mayo is closing out the season with three excellent months. Henderson has been hitting well since about mid-August and has maintained value with solid shortstop defense – that's not to say it's flawless, but the good has outweighed the bad even in what is another disappointing year for him overall. For Bradish, I don't know. It felt good when he got that contract extension.
For me, Alonso is at the top, followed by Young and Rogers. Young's surprisingly-good season was probably the only thing that prevented the Orioles from being completely buried in May or June. The team is 19-8 in Young starts this year. Whoever voted for Baz clearly didn't hold the team's 10-21 record in his starts against him. Baz probably "deserves" like 15-16 in his starts.
After Alonso and Young, you can make the case for a lot of people as third place, and that's reflected in the variety of names who also received votes. Rogers was not good in April and May but has looked like a fringe Cy Young candidate ever since. That picks up on last year, when he was a Cy Young-caliber pitcher in the 18 starts that he made. That's why I'd pick him for the third place spot; Rogers was the MVO winner a year ago.
Somebody's going to pay Rogers this offseason. I don't have any hope that it will be the Orioles.

BALTIMORE -- Every season, one Baltimore player receives the Most Valuable Oriole Award, an honor that is voted on by members of the local print and broadcast media who cover the team on a regular basis. And some years, it can be a difficult decision resulting in a close race.
That was not the case in 2026.
Pete Alonso was unanimously named the winner of this year’s Most Valuable Oriole Award, the club announced Wednesday. The 31-year-old slugger was the runaway favorite for the recognition, as he was clearly the team’s top player during his first season in Baltimore.
Ballots included up to three players, with points tabulated in a 5-3-1 format (for first, second and third, respectively). The other O’s players to receive votes this year were utility man Blaze Alexander, catcher Samuel Basallo, right-hander Shane Baz, right-hander Kyle Bradish, infielder Christian Encarnacion-Strand, right-hander Rico Garcia, shortstop Gunnar Henderson, infielder Coby Mayo, left-hander Trevor Rogers and right-hander Brandon Young.
But nobody was coming close to Alonso, who has lived up to lofty expectations since signing a five-year, $155 million deal to join the Orioles last December.
Alonso has been racking up honors of late, as he was the Orioles’ nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award and also their recipient of the Heart & Hustle Award. Now, he’s the Most Valuable Oriole -- the first unanimous winner since outfielder Cedric Mullins in 2021 -- and it wouldn’t be surprising if he finishes quite high in American League MVP Award voting after his strong conclusion to the season.
Entering Wednesday, Alonso led Baltimore in hits (156), runs scored (94), home runs (40), RBIs (108), batting average (.265), slugging percentage (.510) and OPS (.869). He’s also the only O’s player to start all 157 games this season.
All of the numbers are impressive. But Alonso’s power and run production have stood out most.
Now sitting at 304 career home runs, Alonso has clubbed at least 37 homers in six of his eight MLB seasons and has reached the 40-homer mark four times. The Polar Bear is the ninth player in Orioles history (since 1954) to hit 40 in a season, marking the 10th overall occurrence.
Alonso’s 108 RBIs are the most in the AL. He is on pace to become the first player in AL/NL history to post a season in which he led the league in RBIs in both leagues. (Alonso had a National League-high 131 RBIs for the Mets in 2022.)
The stats have never been the most important thing to Alonso, though.
“I just want to leave it all out there,” Alonso recently said. “I really love playing the game, and for me, I just want to be all I can be and do whatever I can every single night to win the game, you know? I really take pride in wanting to win and giving it all I have.”
The Orioles (76-81 entering Wednesday) are unlikely to reach the postseason, as they’re close to elimination. But Alonso has four more years remaining on his contract and is hopeful he can lead the club back to the playoffs as soon as possible.

OF Chuck Diering (1954)
OF Dave Philley (1955)
RHP Stu Miller (1963)
OF Frank Robinson (1966)
OF Ken Singleton (1975)
RHP Rodrigo Lopez (2002, rookie)
SS Miguel Tejada (2004)
DH Nelson Cruz (2014)
C Adley Rutschman (2022, rookie)
1B Pete Alonso (2026)
Alonso has hit well, played strong defense at first base and become a leader inside Baltimore’s clubhouse. He’s been an even better fit with the O’s than those in the organization could have imagined he’d be this past winter.
“My belief on any long-term contract is, if you’re going to do anything over three years -- especially when you get into the five-year, 10-year range -- that person has to have behaviors that impact the environment. You want that guy to have a compound effect where he gets people better,” bench coach Donnie Ecker said. “Pete’s up there with the best I’ve seen, just in terms of caring for the people around him and really not ever settling for average.”

He will be recognized for his accomplishments during an on-field ceremony prior to tonight’s game against the Toronto Blue Jays.
Alonso is the eighth first baseman (18th instance) in franchise history to be named Most Valuable Oriole, joining JIM GENTILE (1961), BOOG POWELL (1969-1970), LEE MAY (1976), EDDIE MURRAY (1978, 1981-1985, and 1988), RAFAEL PALMEIRO (1995-1996 and 1998), JEFF CONINE (2001), and CHRIS DAVIS (2013 and 2015). He is also the first to be named the unanimous winner of the award since CEDRIC MULLINS in 2021.
The right-handed slugger is slashing .265/.359/.510 (156-for-588) with 24 doubles, 40 home runs, 94 runs, 108 RBI, 78 walks (5 IBB), 11 hit-by-pitches, and five stolen bases, starting all 157 games for the Orioles this season. He enters play today leading the American League in RBI while ranking third in homers, third in total bases (300), fifth in slugging percentage, fifth in OPS (.869), sixth in extra-base hits (64), seventh in hits, and eighth in runs. He paces all Orioles hitters in hits, homers, runs, RBI, total bases, and extra-base hits. Alonso has played in 573 consecutive games, the second-longest active streak in the majors behind Atlanta’s Matt Olson (939 G).
The 31-year-old leads the Orioles with 4.6 Baseball Reference Wins Above Replacement (bWAR) and 4.5 Fangraphs Wins Above Replacement (fWAR), ranking first among all MLB first basemen in fWAR. His 4.6 bWAR is the highest by an Orioles first baseman since CHRIS DAVIS (4.9 bWAR) in 2015.
Alonso earned AL Player of the Week honors for the week of August 10-16 when he slashed .545/.630/.864 (12-for-22) with one double, two home runs, five runs, five RBI, and four walks in six games played. He was the first Oriole to earn the honor since GUNNAR HENDERSON on September 7, 2024, and the first Orioles first baseman since RYAN MOUNTCASTLE on June 5, 2021.
This season, he became the eighth Oriole to hit at least 30 home runs in his first season with the team, joining FRANK ROBINSON (49 in 1966), MARK TRUMBO (47 in 2016), NELSON CRUZ (40 in 2014), MARK REYNOLDS (37 in 2011), ALBERT BELLE (37 in 1999), MIGUEL TEJADA (34 in 2004), and J.J. HARDY (30 in 2011). He also became the fifth player in MLB history to hit 30+ home runs in at least seven of his first eight seasons, joining Mark Teixeira, Albert Pujols, Eddie Mathews, and Ralph Kiner. The Most Valuable Oriole Award is named in honor of the late LOU HATTER, a former sportswriter for The Baltimore Sun who covered the Orioles for 27 years. By LUKE OLSON Associated Press
SEATTLE (AP) — Yordan Alvarez resumed his Triple Crown push with a home run and three RBIs as the Houston Astros beat the Seattle Mariners 7-0 on Tuesday night to pull even with Texas atop the AL West.
Houston snapped a three-game skid and tied the Rangers at 78-79 following their 6-3 loss to the New York Mets at home. Both teams have five games remaining, and the Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Seattle (73-84) is on the brink of playoff elimination, one season after winning the AL West for the first time in 24 years and coming within one victory of the franchise’s first World Series appearance.
Alvarez hit a two-run drive to right field in the eighth inning to tie Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays for the American League lead with 41 homers. Alvarez is first in batting average at .314 and he has 102 RBIs, six behind Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso for most in the AL.
Miguel Cabrera of the Detroit Tigers in 2012 was the most recent hitter to win a Triple Crown by leading his league in all three of those statistical categories.
Alvarez hit an RBI single in the first to reach 100 RBIs for the second time in his career. Christian Walker belted a three-run homer to make it 4-0 in the third, and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot in the sixth.
It was the 200th home run of Walker’s career and his 26th this season.
Cam Smith snapped an 0-for-26 skid with a double.
Houston starter Cristian Javier was removed after two innings with right groin tightness. He threw 45 pitches. Miguel Ullola (1-0) followed with two innings of one-hit ball for his first major league win.
Bennett Sousa, AJ Blubaugh and Logan VanWey completed the four-hitter.
Mariners starter Logan Gilbert (12-11) lasted only four innings, yielding four runs on 10 hits — the most hits he’s allowed in a game this season.
Up next
Rookie right-hander Ethan Pecko (1-0, 3.77 ERA) makes his fifth major league start Wednesday for Houston against Seattle RHP George Kirby (9-11, 4.24).

Pete Alonso has spent much of the last week going viral, much to Baltimore Orioles fans’ pleasure and New York Mets fans’ … well, we’d call it dismay, but Citi Field viewed things far differently.
Alonso has since left New York in more ways than one, and the Orioles are back in Charm City for their final home series. The five-time All-Star hit his 39th and 40th homers in Monday’s 4-3 win over the Blue Jays, becoming only the ninth player in franchise history to join such a club.
Fans might dig the long ball, but Alonso has done far more than round the bases so frequently. He entered Tuesday leading the American League with 108 RBIs, and he's only three behind the Cardinals' Alec Burleson for the most in the majors. Despite a relatively slow start, the veteran first baseman has a healthy lead over the Astros' Yordan Alvarez (99) and Rays' Junior Caminero (97) with six games left.
All of that sounds great, but here’s the kicker: At his current pace, Alonso would become the first player in MLB history to lead the AL and NL in RBIs in two separate seasons; he and Aaron Judge tied for an MLB-high 131 RBIs in 2022.
Pete Alonso continues to further humiliate Steve Cohen’s New York Mets
First off, can we just appreciate the fact that no player has ever won the RBI title in separate leagues? You’d think Frank Robinson would have done it seeing as he became the first player to win the MVP in both the AL and NL, but apparently not. Our dark horse pick would have been Mark McGwire.
Alonso’s 4.6 bWAR is his highest since 2019, and he's on track to finish with career highs in on-base percentage (.359) and walk rate (11.4 percent). He cleared the 300-homer mark last week and is currently at 304, so he stands an excellent chance at reaching 400 within the coming years.
All of this follows the Mets allegedly not making Alonso — their all-time home run leader and one of the most beloved players in the post-David Wright era — a formal contract offer this past offseason. Steve Cohen and David Stearns instead opted for Jorge Polanco, who hit .148 with a .431 OPS and -1.4 bWAR over 37 games. Great job, all.
The concerns about how Alonso would age as a power-heavy first baseman were valid, but not offering him a contract easily ranks among the worst decisions in Mets history. You don’t let one of your all-time greats leave without a fight, especially not when he’s still playing at an All-Star level. It’s not like Alonso had a realistic chance to receive $300 million on the open market.
But “what could have been” is the story of the New York Mets’ existence. How far would they have gone in the postseason had they not collapsed in 2007, 2008, and 2025? Would Tom Seaver have helped the Mets return to form rather than join the Reds in the “Midnight Massacre?”
At least Alonso seemingly landed in a place where leadership respects him — and if they’re smart, they’ll consult him on any potential offseason moves. Here’s an idea: Do everything that the Mets wouldn’t do.

SEATTLE (AP) — Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez gained some ground Tuesday night in his chase for a Triple Crown.
He still has plenty of work to do this week.
The AL MVP front-runner went 2 for 4 with his 41st home run and three RBIs in the Astros' 7-0 win over the Seattle Mariners. Alvarez hit an RBI single in the first inning, was intentionally walked in the second and then belted a 386-foot homer in the eighth with a 109.5 mph exit velocity.
“At this point, I keep wondering why guys are pitching to him,” Houston first baseman Christian Walker said. “He just seems to come through in every moment. He's dangerous at the plate right now.”
Alvarez, who is quiet and shows little emotion, orchestrated a team meeting after the Astros (78-79) were swept by Atlanta on Sunday, squandering their lead in the AL West. His performance on Tuesday was much-needed to put Houston in a tie with the Texas Rangers atop the division with five games left this season.
“He's been backing it up all year,” Astros manager Joe Espada said.
Alvarez's two-run shot to right field tied him with Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays for the American League lead with 41 homers. Alvarez is first in batting average at .314 — five points ahead of Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson — and he has 102 RBIs, six behind Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso for most in the AL.
Alonso drove in three runs with two homers Monday against Toronto, but the teams were rained out Tuesday in Baltimore because of bad weather. They are scheduled to play a split doubleheader Wednesday.
Alvarez has six homers since Aug. 1, and the 29-year-old designated hitter has eight RBIs over 17 games in September. He'll need more to become baseball’s first Triple Crown winner since Miguel Cabrera in 2012.
Alvarez leads the AL in slugging percentage (.601), OPS (1.032), total bases (329) and walks (106). Logan Gilbert intentionally walked Alvarez in the second inning Tuesday, which was the 33rd time for Alvarez this season, already a franchise record.
It’s been a historic season for the four-time All-Star after he was limited to 48 games in 2025 because of a broken hand and an ankle injury.
If he wins the AL MVP award, the Cuban slugger will join Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers as the only players to win an MVP award while primarily serving as a designated hitter. Othani was close to winning a Triple Crown in 2024 after leading the NL in homers (50) and RBIs (130), but his .310 average fell just short to Luis Arráez’s .314.

El primera base de los Orioles está cerca de alcanzar un registro que no tiene registro desde hace más de un siglo en las Grandes Ligas
Pete Alonso está cerca de conseguir una marca inédita en la historia de las Grandes Ligas. El primera base de los Orioles de Baltimore tiene la oportunidad de convertirse en el primer jugador en más de un siglo de MLB que termina como líder de carreras impulsadas en ambas ligas, una estadística oficial que se tiene registro desde 1920.
El Oso Polar vive una temporada destacada con Baltimore y llega a la recta final del calendario como uno de los principales productores ofensivos de la Liga Americana. Su objetivo es completar una hazaña que ningún pelotero ha logrado desde la creación de las Grandes Ligas modernas.
La posibilidad de Alonso tiene como antecedente su rendimiento cuando formaba parte de la Liga Nacional. El toletero ya consiguió encabezar ese departamento en 2022 con los Mets de Nueva York y ahora busca repetir la hazaña del otro lado de la MLB con los Mets de Nueva York.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Justin Verlander prepara su última apertura en las Grandes Ligas
Alonso busca dominar las carreras impulsadas en ambas ligas
El reto de Pete Alonso está relacionado con su capacidad para producir carreras, una de las principales características que ha mostrado durante su trayectoria en las Grandes Ligas.
El primera base llegó a la temporada 2026 con una carrera consolidada como uno de los bateadores de mayor poder en MLB y ahora tiene la oportunidad de sumar un logro que ningún jugador ha alcanzado en 106 años de historia.
Durante su etapa anterior en la Liga Nacional, Alonso logró posicionarse como uno de los mejores productores ofensivos del circuito con 131 carreras impulsadas. Ahora, con los Orioles, busca repetir ese dominio en la Liga Americana.
De acuerdo con los registros históricos, ningún pelotero ha terminado una temporada como líder de carreras impulsadas en ambas ligas, por lo que Alonso podría convertirse en el primero en conseguirlo.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Alex Bregman recibe pelotazo en el rostro y abandona juego
Una temporada histórica con los Orioles
Pete Alonso llegó a Baltimore como una de las principales incorporaciones ofensivas del equipo y rápidamente asumió un papel importante dentro del orden al bate. El jugador ha mantenido su capacidad para generar extrabases y producir carreras, características que lo han acompañado desde su debut en MLB en 2019.
Además de su producción ofensiva, Alonso continúa ampliando su legado dentro del béisbol profesional. En 2026 también alcanzó una marca importante al llegar a los 300 cuadrangulares en su carrera, logro que consiguió como jugador de los Orioles frente a los Mets, su antiguo equipo.
Alonso busca entrar en la historia de MLB
La recta final de la temporada será determinante para conocer si Pete Alonso consigue completar una de las hazañas más difíciles del béisbol moderno. A menos de una semana de finalizar su primera temporada con los Orioles de Baltimore, Pete Alonso se mantiene en la pelea por una marca histórica. El primera base suma 108 carreras impulsadas, nueve más que el cubano Yordan Álvarez, quien acumula 99 y ocupa el segundo lugar de la Liga Americana en este departamento.
Con la recta final del calendario por disputarse, Alonso tiene una ventaja importante para quedarse con el liderato de impulsadas. Salvo que Álvarez tenga una última semana extraordinaria, el jugador de Baltimore podría terminar la campaña en la cima de este rubro y acercarse a una hazaña que no se consigue desde hace más de un siglo.

Pete Alonso has been everything the Baltimore Orioles could have hoped for since signing him to a five-year, $155 million deal in the offseason.
Alonso hit his 39th and 40th home runs in Monday night's win over the Toronto Blue Jays. Some teams were reportedly hesitant to pay Alonso in free agency because they were unsure if he could maintain his power numbers as he got older. Well, in Year 1 of his new deal, he has shown no signs of slowing down. He is also hitting .265 this season.
His 40th home run for the Orioles carries some historical significance. Alonso hit 53 home runs in his rookie year on the New York Mets in the National League. His 40th home run in his first year as part of an American League team makes him the only player in MLB history to hit at least 40 home runs in his first season in each league, according to OptaSTATS.
Since 2019, when Alonso made his debut, only Kyle Schwarber has hit more home runs than him. Schwarber is two years older than Alonso and may be a good example of how Alonso will age. Schwarber strikes out a ton and does not have a good batting average. However, he hits home runs at a very high clip and is currently tied for the most home runs in baseball.
Alonso and the Orioles may not make the postseason, but Alonso proved he deserved to be paid handsomely and should be a key player for the Orioles in the near future as they look to get back to playing baseball in October.

Happy Tuesday, Camden Chatters!
Last night, we got a reprieve from the misery that has been Orioles baseball lately. And we got it mostly thanks to Pete Alonso (who else). Alonso hit his 39th and 40th home runs of the season last night, powering the Orioles to a 4-3 victory over the Blue Jays. He's now the 10th Oriole to have a 40-homer season, and his 108 RBI are the most in the American League. It's Alonso's first 40-homer season since 2023 and his fourth in his career.
Oh, and Alonso just happened to hit two homers on the day that his son, Teddy, celebrated his first birthday. What a guy.
Gunnar Henderson also homered, his 24th. Henderson had three hits in the game. Starting pitcher Shane Baz struggled through a three-run first inning, but went on to pitch 6.2 innings without allowing a run after the first. You can get the full details of the win in Alex Church's recap.
By my estimation, the Orioles have been out of the race since the Red Sox swept them in early September. Now it seems like the White Sox or Guardians will take the final Wild Card spot, with the other winning the AL Central. The Blue Jays are basically out of it as well, and the Orioles have the chance in this series to ensure their AL East foe is truly finished.
The Orioles won't go to the playoffs and they won't have a winning season, but they can put the nail in the coffin for the Blue Jays. And if the Orioles win tonight and tomorrow, these teams will leave Baltimore with the Blue Jays in last place instead of the Orioles. It's not something to get excited about, but it's always preferable to NOT be in last place.
Tonight, it'll be an old-man special as Chris Bassitt (37) and Max Scherzer (42) face off. It's a rematch of the game on 9/11, in which both pitchers went five innings. Scherzer allowed six runs and took the loss, while Bassitt allowed two runs and got the win. I wouldn't hate to see a repeat of that. The weather forecast today is pretty dicey, so hopefully they get the game in. I mean, I guess. Would it really matter if they didn't?

How one swing exposed a season's worth of frustration for the Orioles – The Baltimore Banner
This was written about what happened after the Orioles lost on Sunday, but the contents have been a hot topic in Birdland. Specifically, how Craig Albernaz reacted to the press after Jeremiah Jackson grounded out on the first pitch against a struggling pitcher.
Alonso homers twice to reach 40 and give Orioles 4-3 win over Blue Jays – MASN Sports
Roch Kubatko's game story has plenty of quotes about how amazing Pete Alonso is, but also includes some info on Samuel Basallo, who exited last night's game after being hit square in the mask with a foul ball. Be ok, Samuel! Knocks to the head are scary.

The two awardees were at Camden Yards last night to accept, and both hopped into the broadcast booth to talk about their seasons. If you've never heard those two names spoken aloud before, here is your lesson. Wahiwa is pronounced Vuh-Hee-Vah. Dzierwa is pronounced Jer-Wah. Got it?
Birthdays and History
Is today your birthday? Happy birthday! You have a ton of Orioles birthday buddies, each more forgettable than the last. But because today is their birthday, today we remember them:
- Chris Ellis (34), eight games in 2021-22
- Luis García (51), six games in 2002
- César Devarez (57), 16 games in 1995-96.
- P.J. Forbes (59), nine games in 1998
- John Stefero (67), 61 games in 1983 and 1986
- Bob Harrison (b. 1930, d. 2023), two games in 1955-56
On this day in 1961, Jim Gentile hit his fifth grand slam of the year. That tied him with Ernie Banks for the most in a season. The current record is six, held by Travis Hafner and Don Mattingly.
In 1966, the Orioles clinched their first AL pennant with 6-1 victory over the Kansas City Athletics. Jim Palmer, just 20 years old, pitched a complete game.
In 1973, the Orioles defeated the Milwaukee Brewers 7-1 to clinch the division. Al Bumbry hit three triples in the win.
In 2012, the Orioles beat the Red Sox 9-6 in 13 innings, marking their 87th win of the year. They scored three runs in the top of the 13th with RBI hits from Jim Thome, Endy Chavez, and Manny Machado. Mark Reynolds and Adam Jones homered earlier. They remained one game out of the AL East after the Yankees pulled off an extra-innings win of their own.

Pete Alonso’s second home run of the game and 40th of the season lifted the Baltimore Orioles to a 4-3 comeback victory against the visiting Toronto Blue Jays in the opener of a three-game series Monday night.
Alonso’s two-run shot with two outs in the eighth inning gave Baltimore its first lead of the game. The Orioles pulled within 4 1/2 games of the White Sox in the race for the third American League wild card, while the Blue Jays now trail Chicago by 3 1/2 games.
Alonso also homered in the first inning and Gunnar Henderson (3-for-4) went deep in the sixth inning as the Orioles ended a three-game losing streak. Baltimore reliever Yennier Cano (4-3) worked 1 1/3 shutout innings, and Rico Garcia pitched a 1-2-3 ninth for his 10th save.
George Springer had two singles and an RBI for the Blue Jays, who lost for the fifth time in seven games. Tyler Rogers (2-3) gave up the decisive home run.
Tigers 9, Nationals 2
Ben Malgeri hit a three-run home run, Javier Baez and Spencer Torkelson each supplied two-run shots and host Detroit opened a three-game series with a romp over Washington.
River Ryan, elevated from Triple-A, started and pitched three scoreless innings while recording three strikeouts in his Tigers debut. Ryan, acquired in August from the Dodgers in the Tarik Skubal deal, last pitched in the majors in 2024. Keider Montero (10-9) followed with four shutout innings while striking out five.
Pinch hitter Yohandy Morales produced a two-run homer for the Nationals, who took their second loss in a row. DJ Herz (0-1) allowed four runs in four innings during his first major league outing since 2024.

Drew Gilbert homered, collected three hits and drove in a career-high-tying three runs as host San Francisco defeated Minnesota.
Brett Harris chipped in two hits, including a two-run single, as the Giants snapped a three-game losing streak. San Francisco reliever Tristan Beck (1-0) threw 2 2/3 innings of hitless ball, and Trent Harris tossed a perfect ninth inning for his second save.
Brooks Lee and Emmanuel Rodriguez homered for the Twins, who lost for the sixth time in nine games. Zebby Matthews (9-11) fanned nine in five innings but yielded five runs on eight hits.
